claim: Patch-clamp is the most commonly used technique to monitor neuronal membrane potential.
source: To date, patch-clamp (Neher and Sakmann, 1976) is the most commonly used technique to monitor neuronal membrane potential.
evidence: Supported by citation to Neher and Sakmann, 1976

claim: It remains challenging to monitor the activity of a cell at more than one or two sites using patch-clamp.
source: Despite its unquestionable utility, it remains challenging to monitor the activity of a cell at more than one or two sites.
evidence: Stated as a known limitation of the technique

claim: Extracellular recordings deliver a more global picture of neural activity than patch-clamp.
source: Extracellular recordings, on the other hand, deliver a more global picture of neural activity (Buzsáki et al., 2012; Einevoll et al., 2013a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Buzsáki et al., 2012 and Einevoll et al., 2013a

claim: Modern multielectrodes and microelectrode arrays can record neuronal activity from many thousands of channels.
source: With modern multielectrodes and microelectrode arrays, it is now possible to record neuronal activity from many thousands of channels (Buzsáki, 2004; Berdondini et al., 2005; Obien et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Buzsáki, 2004; Berdondini et al., 2005; Obien et al., 2014

claim: Extracellular recording does not permit direct recording of membrane potentials.
source: However, this technique does not permit direct recording of membrane potentials but instead spiking activity [which may be of individual cells (single-unit activity, SUA) or multiple cells (multiunit activity or MUA, which is the mean firing rate of cell populations)] and components of postsynaptic activity visible at low frequencies (<300 Hz, so-called local field potential, LFP)
evidence: Stated as a characteristic of the technique

claim: High-density array recordings have improved resolution of spike detection.
source: So far, the main advantages of high-density array recordings have been improved resolution of spike detection (Rey et al., 2015), as more cells can be identified in a single recording
evidence: Supported by citation to Rey et al., 2015

claim: High-density probes have been used in studies of axon tracking.
source: Recently, high-density probes have also been used in studies of axon tracking (Bakkum et al., 2013; Lewandowska et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Bakkum et al., 2013 and Lewandowska et al., 2016

claim: Multielectrode recordings have been traditionally used for improved spike sorting.
source: Multielectrode recordings have been traditionally used for improved spike sorting (Buzsáki, 2004; Berdondini et al., 2005; Obien et al., 2014; Muthmann et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to Buzsáki, 2004; Berdondini et al., 2005; Obien et al., 2014; Muthmann et al., 2015

claim: Multielectrode recordings have been used for reconstruction of current source densities behind recorded LFP.
source: Multielectrode recordings have been traditionally used for improved spike sorting (Buzsáki, 2004; Berdondini et al., 2005; Obien et al., 2014; Muthmann et al., 2015) and for the reconstruction of current source densities (CSD) behind the recorded LFP (Pitts, 1952; Mitzdorf, 1985; Wójcik, 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to Pitts, 1952; Mitzdorf, 1985; Wójcik, 2015

claim: The authors are not aware of any prior attempts to reconstruct the CSD of individual neurons using their available morphologies.
source: We are not aware of any prior attempts, however, to reconstruct the CSD of individual neurons using their available morphologies, which we propose here.
evidence: Authors state their lack of awareness of prior work

claim: The skCSD method assumes a set of extracellular recordings from a specific neuron whose morphology and location with respect to the electrode is known.
source: This method assumes we have a set of extracellular recordings, coming from a specific neuron, whose morphology and location with respect to the electrode is known, collected with multiple contacts.
evidence: Stated as an assumption of the method

claim: The data necessary to apply the skCSD method have been available for some time.
source: The data necessary to apply presented method have been available for some time (Henze et al., 2000; Gold et al., 2006), although recently have became much more comprehensive (Jäckel et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Henze et al., 2000; Gold et al., 2006; Jäckel et al., 2017

claim: The estimation of transmembrane currents along the cell morphology using extracellular recordings has not been reported previously.
source: While we believe the estimation of transmembrane currents along the cell morphology using this type of data has not been reported previously, similar questions have been posed by (Gold et al., 2006)
evidence: Authors state their belief based on literature review

claim: The skCSD method is an application of the kernel Current Source Density method framework to data coming from a single cell.
source: The single-cell kernel Current Source Density method (skCSD) we introduce here is an application of the framework of the kernel Current Source Density method (Potworowski et al., 2012) to the data coming from a single cell.
evidence: Stated as the basis of the method with citation to Potworowski et al., 2012

claim: The skCSD method restricts current sources to cell morphology.
source: This is done by restricting current sources to cell morphology.
evidence: Stated as a key feature of the method

claim: The skCSD method can be applied efficiently for arbitrarily complex morphologies and arbitrary electrode configurations.
source: This can be done efficiently for arbitrarily complex morphologies and arbitrary electrode configurations.
evidence: Stated as a capability of the method

claim: For the first time, this work shows how a collection of extracellular recordings in combination with cell morphology can be used to estimate how current sources on a studied cell contribute to the recorded field potential.
source: The importance of this work is that for the first time we show here how a collection of extracellular recordings in combination with cell morphology can be used to estimate how the current sources located on a studied cell contribute to the recorded field potential.
evidence: Authors claim novelty of their contribution

claim: The proposed method can be used to constrain the biophysical properties of the neuron membrane.
source: Since it is feasible to acquire the relevant data, we believe that the method proposed here may be used to constrain the biophysical properties of the neuron membrane and facilitate consistency of the reconstructed morphology.
evidence: Authors speculate on potential applications

claim: The proposed method can facilitate consistency of the reconstructed morphology.
source: Since it is feasible to acquire the relevant data, we believe that the method proposed here may be used to constrain the biophysical properties of the neuron membrane and facilitate consistency of the reconstructed morphology.
evidence: Authors speculate on potential applications

claim: Increasing the density and number of electrodes improves spatial resolution of the skCSD method.
source: As shown in Figure 2, with 128 electrodes it is possible to reconstruct higher frequency distributions as compared to eight electrodes.
evidence: Demonstrated through simulation results shown in Figure 2

claim: Denser probing of extracellular space leads to higher spatial precision in skCSD reconstruction.
source: Increasing the density of electrodes within the studied region leads to higher spatial precision.
evidence: Stated as an observation from the results

claim: The skCSD method can recover synaptic activations from extracellular recordings.
source: As can be seen, the reconstructed CSD distribution reflects the ground-truth, and the precision of reconstruction improves with an increasing number of contacts, which is reflected in the reduction of cross-validation error.
evidence: Demonstrated through simulation results in Figure 3

claim: The skCSD method provides more detail about membrane CSD than interpolated LFP and standard CSD analyses in cases where those are not informative.
source: We also wanted to determine if this method provides more detail about the current distribution on the cell than what is accessible from the interpolated potential and the CSD reconstructed with kCSD under the assumption of a smooth distribution of sources in space, which is the natural approach to try (Frey et al., 2009).
evidence: Demonstrated through comparison in Figure 5

claim: The skCSD reconstruction is not sensitive to specific selection of electrode placement.
source: Note that in certain cases, the random distribution is more efficient than the regular grid, which is probably due to more fortunate samplings of the area covered by the morphology.
evidence: Demonstrated through simulation results in Figure 6

claim: Significant additive noise (SNR = 1) is not prohibitive for skCSD reconstruction.
source: As can be seen in the reconstruction plots (Figure 9D–F), the increasing noise actually does not seem to significantly alter the obtained reconstructions so the regularization is providing adequate correction, except for the noise on the order of signal (Figure 9F).
evidence: Demonstrated through simulation results in Figure 9

claim: The quality of skCSD reconstruction improves with the coverage of the morphology by the electrodes.
source: The results obtained in this study are consistent with our expectations: the quality of reconstruction improves with the coverage of the morphology by the electrodes, with increasing density of probing, and with increasing number of probes (Figure 10I).
evidence: Demonstrated through simulation results in Figure 10

claim: The quality of skCSD reconstruction improves with increasing density of probing.
source: The results obtained in this study are consistent with our expectations: the quality of reconstruction improves with the coverage of the morphology by the electrodes, with increasing density of probing, and with increasing number of probes (Figure 10I).
evidence: Demonstrated through simulation results in Figure 10

claim: The quality of skCSD reconstruction improves with increasing number of probes.
source: The results obtained in this study are consistent with our expectations: the quality of reconstruction improves with the coverage of the morphology by the electrodes, with increasing density of probing, and with increasing number of probes (Figure 10I).
evidence: Demonstrated through simulation results in Figure 10

claim: The skCSD method performed adequately for proof-of-concept experimental data.
source: The skCSD method performed adequately for the proof-of-concept experimental data, even if the nature of the experiment allowed only the reconstruction of the general features of the spike-triggered average spatio-temporal current source density distribution patterns.
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental results in Figure 11 and Video 2

claim: At 0.45 ms after spike threshold crossing, the extracellular potential on the second electrode reaches its minimum.
source: The extracellular potential on the second electrode reaches its minimum at 0.45 ms, which signals the peak of the spike.
evidence: Observed in experimental data analysis

claim: The first CSD method specific for investigating membrane currents on single cells was proposed by Somogyvári et al., 2005.
source: While the traditional (population) CSD method was used to analyze membrane currents of single cells before (Buzsáki and Kandel, 1998; Bereshpolova et al., 2007; Frey et al., 2009), the first CSD method specific for investigating membrane currents on single cells was proposed by (Somogyvári et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Somogyvári et al., 2005

claim: The CSD method by Somogyvári et al., 2005 assumed simplified, linear neuron morphologies.
source: However, it assumed simplified, linear neuron morphologies.
evidence: Stated as a limitation of prior work

claim: The novelty of the skCSD method is in its use of actual neuronal morphologies.
source: The novelty of the skCSD method proposed here is in its use of actual neuronal morphologies and in the underlying algorithmic solutions based on the kCSD method (Potworowski et al., 2012) which were initially used in the study of populations of neurons.
evidence: Authors state the novel aspects of their method

claim: The best way to identify optimal parameters for skCSD reconstruction is by minimizing the L1 error between the reconstruction and the ground truth.
source: We found that the best way to identify optimal parameters for reconstruction is by minimizing the L1 error between the reconstruction and the ground truth.
evidence: Based on simulation studies

claim: The code used for the study is available at https://github.com/csdori/skCSD.
source: We plan to develop and open framework facilitating such studies, meanwhile, the code used for the present study is available at https://github.com/csdori/skCSD (Cserpán, 2017; copy archived at https://github.com/elifesciences-publications/skCSD).
evidence: Authors provide code availability information

claim: Recording extracellular potential with a MEA, filling a neuron with a dye, and reconstructing its morphology are standard experimental techniques.
source: Although recording extracellular potential with a MEA, filling a neuron with a dye, and reconstructing its morphology, are standard experimental techniques, using them simultaneously remains a challenge due to the size of the experimental devices which need to be arranged within a small volume.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: Using MEA recording, dye filling, and morphology reconstruction simultaneously remains a challenge due to the size of experimental devices.
source: Although recording extracellular potential with a MEA, filling a neuron with a dye, and reconstructing its morphology, are standard experimental techniques, using them simultaneously remains a challenge due to the size of the experimental devices which need to be arranged within a small volume.
evidence: Stated as a practical challenge

claim: Intracellular recording less than 100 μm from the MEA is extremely challenging.
source: Although these would be favorable data, intracellular recording less than 100 μm from the MEA is extremely challenging.
evidence: Stated as a practical challenge

claim: Experimental setups featuring the necessary equipment for combined intracellular and MEA recording already exist.
source: Experimental setups featuring the necessary equipment already exist (Neto et al., 2016), but as far as we know, have not been used in this way.
evidence: Supported by citation to Neto et al., 2016

claim: The relation between current sources in tissue and recording potentials is given by the Poisson equation.
source: The relation between current sources in the tissue and the recording potentials is given by the Poisson equation
evidence: Stated as established physics

claim: Walter Pitts observed that for recordings obtained with regular grids one can approximate the Poisson equation to estimate the distribution of current sources in tissue.
source: Already in the middle of the 20th century, Walter H. Pitts observed that for recordings obtained with regular grids one can approximate the Poisson equation to estimate the distribution of current sources in the tissue (Pitts, 1952).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pitts, 1952

claim: The kernel Current Source Density method was proposed in 2012 to overcome the restriction of regular grids.
source: In 2012, we proposed how to overcome the restriction of regular grids with a kernel approach which both allows to use arbitrary distribution of contacts and corrects for noise (Potworowski et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Potworowski et al., 2012

claim: The LFPy package was used to simulate the extracellular potential at arbitrarily placed virtual electrodes.
source: The LFPy package (Lindén et al., 2013) was used to simulate the extracellular potential at arbitrarily placed virtual electrodes.
evidence: Stated as a method with citation to Lindén et al., 2013

claim: The .swc morphology description format was assumed for neuron models.
source: We assumed the .swc morphology description format (Cannon et al., 1998)
evidence: Stated as a method with citation to Cannon et al., 1998

claim: A mouse retinal ganglion cell morphology from NeuroMorpho.Org was used as a realistic example.
source: As a realistic example, we used a mouse retinal ganglion cell morphology (Kong et al., 2005) from NeuroMorpho.Org (Ascoli, 2006).
evidence: Stated as a method with citations to Kong et al., 2005 and Ascoli, 2006

claim: One hundred and fifty-four spikes were detected on the 180 s long intracellular recording.
source: One hundred and fifty-four spikes were detected on the 180 s long intra-cellular recording by 0 mV upward threshold crossing.
evidence: Stated as experimental observation

claim: Two channels of the multielectrode array were broken in the experiment.
source: Two channels were broken (2, 5); however, as the skCSD method allows retrieving CSD maps from arbitrarily distributed contacts, this has not prevented the analysis
evidence: Stated as experimental observation

claim: The morphology loop is a closed curve that covers all segments of the cell.
source: To do this, a one-dimensional parametrization of the cell morphology is needed. This could be done independently for each branch of the neuron or globally for the whole cell at once. While the first approach might seem easier, handling of the branching point is non-trivial. Instead, we decided to fit a closed curve on the morphology, which we call the morphology loop (Figure 1). This curve should cover all the segments of the cell, be as short as possible, and be aligned with the morphology.
evidence: Stated as a methodological choice with reference to Figure 1

claim: The construction of the morphology loop is a special case of the Chinese postman problem from graph theory.
source: We also need a method to handle the branching points and guide the parametrization so that all the branches will be visited in an optimal way. This problem is a special case of the Chinese postman problem known from graph theory (Kwan, 1962).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kwan, 1962

claim: The skCSD method acts locally in time, analyzing the collection of potentials at each moment independently.
source: Not much change is seen in time, which is a consequence of the fact that skCSD, like all the CSD estimation methods, acts locally in time. That is, for every moment in time, the collection of potentials at this time, is analyzed. There is no direct relation to the past or future of the measured signals.
evidence: Stated as a property of the method

claim: The skCSD method can be applied to data coming from a single electrode, though the estimate would be poor.
source: Technically, it can be applied to data coming from a single electrode just like the age profile of a human population can be estimated from a single specimen. Obviously, in both cases, the estimate would be a poor reflection of the distribution of interest.
evidence: Stated as a theoretical possibility with analogy

claim: As sampling improves, the quality of skCSD estimate improves.
source: As we improve the sampling, the quality of the estimate improves, yet ultimately it is hard to judge a priori how many electrodes is enough and if our results obtain the required level of precision.
evidence: Stated as a general principle

claim: The number of basis functions was set to 512 for all cases in this work.
source: In this work, the number of basis function was set to 512 for all cases, which is at least twice the number of electrodes used.
evidence: Stated as a methodological choice

claim: For the basis width, values of 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 μm were tested.
source: For the basis width (Equation. (16)) we took the following values: 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 μm.
evidence: Stated as a methodological choice

claim: The regularization parameter values tested were 0.00001, 0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1.
source: Here, we tested the effect of the regularization parameter taking values of 0.00001, 0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1
evidence: Stated as a methodological choice

claim: The in vitro experiment was performed according to the EC Council Directive of November 24, 1986 (86/89/EEC).
source: The in vitro experiment was performed according to the EC Council Directive of November 24, 1986 (86/89/EEC) and all procedures were reviewed and approved by the local ethical committee and the Hungarian Central Government Office (license number: PEI/001/695-9/2015).
evidence: Stated as compliance with regulations

claim: Horizontal hippocampal slices of 500 µm thickness were cut with a vibratome.
source: Horizontal hippocampal slices of 500 µm thickness were cut with a vibratome (VT1200s; Leica, Nussloch, Germany).
evidence: Stated as experimental method

claim: A 16-channel linear multielectrode was used for extracellular local field potential recordings.
source: For the extracellular local field potential recordings, we used a 16-channel linear multielectrode (A16 × 1–2 mm-50-177-A16, Neuronexus Technologies, Ann Arbor, MI)
evidence: Stated as experimental method

claim: Wideband signals (0.1−7500 Hz) were recorded with a sampling frequency of 20 kHz and with 16-bit resolution.
source: Wideband signals (0.1−7500 Hz) were recorded with a sampling frequency of 20 kHz and with 16-bit resolution.
evidence: Stated as experimental method

claim: The recorded neuron was held by a constant −40 nA current injection.
source: The recorded neuron was held by a constant −40 nA current injection.
evidence: Stated as experimental method
